tip: ada isn't 'have' here – it marks that something is somewhere: kantor pos ada di sebelah kanan = the post office is (exists) on the right. Indonesian drops 'is', but location keeps ada.
Descriptions follow the noun and 'that' comes last: tas hitam itu = bag-black-that. English order is reversed – itu always closes the phrase.
The owner follows the thing owned: mobil saya = car-my. No 's and no 'of' – just put the possessor right after the noun it belongs to.
jam goes before the number for clock time: jam sembilan = nine o'clock. Flip it to sembilan jam and it means nine hours – the order decides which.
No do/does shuffle in questions: berapa lama (how long) just sits where the answer would – Dari sini ke bandara berapa lama? The word order never moves.
Verbs never change for tense – sudah does the work: sudah mengirim = have already sent. Drop sudah and the same sentence could be present or future.
dia is both 'he' and 'she' – Indonesian pronouns ignore gender. Dia sedang bekerja could describe anyone; only context tells you who.
kami means 'we, not including you': kantor kami = our office, but not yours. If the listener is part of the group, Indonesian switches to kita.
